title: Cooperative & Group Enterprise Management
subtitle: Run a women's group enterprise as a true cooperative, with sound bylaws, clear roles, checked books and fair sharing of surplus.
description: An advanced, hands-on course for women who lead or are building a producer or service cooperative. It teaches the International Cooperative Alliance definition, values and seven principles, then turns them into bylaws, roles, quality and money controls, bulk-order costing, patronage refunds, safe contracts, member exits and a well-run AGM.
outcomes: Test any group against the ICA definition, values and seven cooperative principles
Choose a suitable legal form in Nigeria and score the group's readiness to register
Draft bylaws with membership, quorum, voting, spending limits and surplus rules
Set up separated roles, an order procedure, a quality check and a monthly bank reconciliation
Cost a bulk order, check capacity, and allocate surplus with patronage refunds that add up
Test a large buyer's offer for working capital and autonomy, and run an AGM with a 90-day governance plan
audience: Women who lead, manage or are forming a cooperative or group enterprise and want it to grow without breaking apart.
tools: A smartphone with WhatsApp and a calculator app
A notebook or a simple spreadsheet (Google Sheets or Excel)
Your group's current agreement, cashbook and bank statements, if you have them
Access to your group's bank account statements for the reconciliation practice

modules.title: Cooperative Identity, Legal Form and the Group Agreement
modules.overview: Start with what a cooperative actually is, using the internationally agreed definition, values and seven principles of the International Cooperative Alliance. Then choose the right legal form for your group in Nigeria and write the bylaws that will hold it together when money and pressure grow.

lessons.title: The cooperative identity: definition, values and the seven principles
objectives: State the ICA definition of a cooperative and explain each of its key words
Name the six cooperative values and four ethical values
Explain the seven cooperative principles in your own words with a local example
Score your own group against the seven principles and find its weakest point

blocks.text: Many groups in Nigeria call themselves a cooperative: a thrift group, a market women's association, a farmers' union, a set of tailors sharing one shop. Some of them truly are cooperatives. Others are a business owned by one strong person with friends helping. The difference matters, because the cooperative model gives members rights that the other models do not. This lesson gives you the exact standard used around the world, so you can test your own group against it.

blocks.name: team-spirit
blocks.alt: A group of people celebrating together
blocks.caption: A cooperative is people, not capital: the members own it, control it and use it.

blocks.text: The definition

The International Cooperative Alliance (ICA) is the global body for cooperatives. Its Statement on the Cooperative Identity, revised in 1995, defines a cooperative as: **"an autonomous association of persons united voluntarily to meet their common economic, social and cultural needs and aspirations through a jointly-owned and democratically-controlled enterprise."** Read it slowly, because every phrase is a test.

items: **Autonomous:** the group runs itself. A politician, a donor or a buyer may support it, but does not control it.
**Association of persons:** it is built around people, not around money. The member with the biggest share does not own more of the decisions.
**United voluntarily:** nobody is forced to join or forced to stay.
**Common economic, social and cultural needs:** members join to meet real shared needs, such as cheaper inputs, a bigger market, training or mutual support.
**Jointly-owned and democratically-controlled enterprise:** it is a real business, owned together and governed by the members.

blocks.text: The values

The ICA statement says cooperatives are based on six values: **self-help, self-responsibility, democracy, equality, equity and solidarity.** Members also hold four ethical values: **honesty, openness, social responsibility and caring for others.** Notice the difference between equality and equity. Equality means every member has the same rights, for example one vote each. Equity means fairness in how members are treated and rewarded, for example sharing surplus according to how much each member used or worked for the cooperative.
The seven principles
The principles are the guidelines by which cooperatives put their values into practice. Below is each one in plain words, with what it looks like in a Nigerian group enterprise.

head: Principle
What it means
What it looks like in practice
rows: Open to all who can use the services and accept the responsibilities, without gender, social, racial, political or religious discrimination
Written admission rules that any qualified woman can meet, not a secret approval by the chairperson's friends
Members set policy and make decisions; elected representatives answer to members; in primary cooperatives, one member, one vote
Officers are elected at a general meeting and can be voted out; a member with more shares still has one vote
Members contribute capital fairly and control it; limited return, if any, on share capital; surplus goes to reserves, to members in proportion to their transactions, or to activities members approve
Every member buys the same entry share; profit is not simply grabbed by whoever has the most money in the group
Agreements with governments, buyers or funders must keep democratic member control
Refusing a grant that would let the donor appoint your treasurer
Train members, elected leaders, managers and staff; inform the public, especially young people and opinion leaders
A budget line for training the new treasurer in bookkeeping
Work with other cooperatives locally, nationally, regionally and internationally
Joining a union of cooperatives to buy inputs in bulk
Work for the sustainable development of communities through policies approved by members
Members vote to fund two apprentices from the community each year

blocks.title: Surplus, not profit
blocks.text: Cooperatives often say surplus instead of profit. The idea is that money left after costs came from the members' own business with the cooperative, so it is returned or reinvested by member decision, not paid out to outside investors.

blocks.title: Worked example: scoring a group against the seven principles
blocks.context: For example, Bisola leads a 14-member school uniform sewing group in Ibadan. Everyone says it is a cooperative. She scores each principle: 2 points if fully true, 1 if partly true, 0 if not true. The maximum is 7 x 2 = 14.
steps: Principle 1, open membership: new members join only if the founder likes them. No written rule. Score 0.
Principle 2, democratic control: there is a chairperson and a secretary, but they were never elected, and the founder decides alone. Score 0.
Principle 3, economic participation: every member paid the same entry share of 20,000 naira, but the surplus has never been calculated or shared. Score 1.
Principle 4, autonomy: the group has no outside controller. Score 2.
Principle 5, education: two members were trained on the industrial machines, but nobody has learnt bookkeeping. Score 1.
Principle 6, cooperation among cooperatives: they buy fabric with another tailoring group once a term. Score 2.
Principle 7, concern for community: they repair torn uniforms free for orphans in their street. Score 2.
blocks.result: The group scores 8 out of 14. Its weakest points are membership rules and democratic control, the two principles that decide who really owns the enterprise. Bisola now knows that the bylaws in Lesson 1.3 must fix admission rules and elections first.

blocks.title: Is it really a cooperative?
items: Open, written membership rules
One member, one vote
Fair capital, shared surplus
Member control kept
Members trained and informed
Works with other cooperatives
Serves the community
blocks.caption: If any of the seven lines is missing, the group is not yet living the cooperative identity, whatever its signboard says.

blocks.title: Use the exact words
blocks.text: When you explain the principles to your members or a funder, quote the ICA wording rather than a summary from social media. The full statement is free on the ICA website, listed in the sources of this course.

takeaways: A cooperative is an autonomous association of persons, jointly owned and democratically controlled
Six values: self-help, self-responsibility, democracy, equality, equity and solidarity
In primary cooperatives every member has one vote, whatever her shares
Surplus goes to reserves, to members in proportion to their transactions, or to member-approved activities
Score your group against all seven principles before you call it a cooperative

activity.title: Score your own group
steps: Write the seven principles on one page, one per line.
Next to each, write one sentence of evidence from your group as it really works today.
Score each principle 2, 1 or 0 and add the total out of 14.
Circle the two lowest scores. These are your priorities for the bylaws lesson.
If you are not yet in a group, score a group you know well, such as a church or market association.
activity.evidence: A one-page scored principles sheet with evidence for each line and the two priorities circled

lessons.title: Choosing a legal form in Nigeria and checking your group's readiness
objectives: Compare an informal group, a registered cooperative society and the CAC registration options
Explain who carries the risk in each form
Run a readiness scorecard on a group before it registers or takes a big order
Decide on a next step based on the score

blocks.text: A group can work together for years without registering anything. That is fine while the money is small. Once the group signs contracts, opens a bank account, borrows, or applies for a grant, the question of legal form becomes urgent: who signs, who owns the equipment, and who pays if something goes wrong? This lesson compares the main options open to a Nigerian women's group enterprise and gives you a readiness check to run before you choose.

blocks.name: contract-signed
blocks.alt: Two people with a signed contract
blocks.caption: Your legal form decides who signs the contract and who carries the risk.

blocks.text: The main options

head: Form
Where it is registered
Key point for a group
rows: Informal group with a written agreement
Cheapest and fastest, but the group is not a legal person. Contracts, bank accounts and debts sit with named individuals, who carry the risk personally.
The government cooperative office of your state (usually a ministry or department responsible for cooperatives)
A legal entity owned and controlled by members on cooperative principles. Comes with duties: bylaws, records, meetings and inspection or audit by the cooperative authorities.
Registers a trading name for one person or partners. It is not a separate legal person, so the owners remain personally liable.
A separate legal person with limited liability. Control usually follows shareholding unless the articles say otherwise, so it does not automatically give one member, one vote.
For associations with non-profit purposes such as charity, religion or education. Not designed for sharing surplus among members.

blocks.title: Check current requirements yourself
blocks.text: Registration requirements, minimum membership numbers and fees differ between states and change over time. Before you register a cooperative society, visit your state's cooperative office in person and ask for the current list of documents and fees in writing. Do not pay an agent who cannot show you an official receipt.
Who carries the risk

In an informal group, if the treasurer signs for a 2 million naira fabric order on credit and the buyer then cancels, the supplier can chase the treasurer personally. Many groups only discover this when it happens. A registered cooperative or a company can enter the contract in its own name, so the obligation sits with the entity, though officers can still be held responsible for fraud or for acting outside their authority. This is the main reason to register once the stakes rise.

A cooperative society also suits a group that wants the cooperative principles written into law: one member, one vote, and surplus returned to members according to their use of the business. A company suits a group where a few people invest most of the capital and expect control in proportion. Many women's groups that start as friends sharing work choose the cooperative route for this reason. Some funders and government programmes also prefer to work with registered groups, but read each programme's own rules rather than assuming.
Readiness before registration

Registration does not create trust; it only gives trust a legal shape. Before registering, or before accepting an order bigger than the group has handled, score the group on eight points. Give 2 points if the point is fully in place, 1 if partly, 0 if missing. The maximum is 16. As a working rule for this course, a group scoring 12 or more is ready to move forward; 8 to 11 should fix its gaps for about 90 days first; below 8 should keep working informally and build basic systems.

items: A written agreement or draft bylaws that members have read and accepted.
Officers chosen by a members' vote, with a fixed term.
A group bank account needing two signatures, not anyone's personal account.
A cashbook or ledger updated at least weekly, which any member may inspect.
Each member's capital contribution recorded with receipts.
Regular meetings with minutes, held at least monthly in the last six months.
At least one real disagreement handled by an agreed process.
A clear product or service the group sells together, with known costs.

blocks.title: Worked example: a readiness score for a dyeing group
blocks.context: For example, Kemi's 11-member adire (tie-dye) group in Abeokuta has been offered a monthly order from a fashion shop and wants to register as a cooperative society first.
steps: Written agreement: a two-page agreement signed by all members. 2 points.
Officers elected: chosen by show of hands two years ago, no fixed term. 1 point.
Group bank account with two signatories: the money sits in the chairperson's personal account. 0 points.
Cashbook updated weekly: kept, but only monthly. 1 point.
Capital contributions recorded: each member paid 15,000 naira with receipts. 2 points.
Monthly meetings with minutes: meetings yes, minutes only sometimes. 1 point.
Disagreement handled by agreed process: a quarrel over dye costs was settled by the elders, not by a written process. 1 point.
Clear product with known costs: yes, costed per piece. 2 points.
blocks.result: With 10 out of 16, Kemi's group should spend about 90 days fixing its gaps before registering: open a group account with two signatories, hold an election with fixed terms, and write minutes at every meeting. These are also the first things a registering officer or a serious buyer will look for.

blocks.title: From working together to registering
items: Work together informally
Write the group agreement
Score readiness out of 16
Fix gaps for 90 days
Visit state cooperative office
Register and adopt bylaws
blocks.caption: Registration comes after the systems work, not before it.

takeaways: An informal group is not a legal person; its officers carry contracts and debts personally
Cooperative societies are registered with your state's cooperative office, not with the CAC
The CAC registers business names, companies and incorporated trustees, each with different control and liability
Score readiness out of 16 before registering or taking a big order
Always get current requirements and fees in writing from the official office

activity.title: Choose your form
steps: List the next three big things your group wants to do, such as a contract, a loan or a grant.
For each, write who would sign and who would carry the risk in your current form.
Score your group on the eight readiness points and add the total out of 16.
Write a one-paragraph decision: stay informal for now, fix gaps for 90 days, or start registration, and why.
Write the three questions you will ask at your state cooperative office.
activity.evidence: A readiness scorecard out of 16 and a one-paragraph legal form decision

lessons.title: Writing bylaws that hold: membership, voting, quorum and money rules
objectives: List the sections that strong cooperative bylaws contain
Set a quorum and a special resolution rule and calculate them for your group
Write clear rules for admitting members, leaving and handling money
Show how authority flows from the general meeting to officers

blocks.text: Bylaws are the rule book of a cooperative. A registered cooperative society must have them, and an informal group should write something very similar as its group agreement. Good bylaws are dull to write and priceless in a crisis. When a member is accused of taking money, when two women both want to be chairperson, or when a big order arrives and someone wants to change the profit sharing, the group opens the bylaws instead of shouting.

blocks.name: signed-document
blocks.alt: A person holding a signed document
blocks.caption: Bylaws turn verbal promises into rules every member signed up to.

blocks.text: What the bylaws must cover

items: **Name, address and objects:** what the cooperative exists to do, for example "to produce and market hand-dyed textiles for members".
**Membership:** who may join, how to apply, entry fee and minimum share, rights and duties, and how membership ends (resignation, death, expulsion).
**General meetings:** the annual general meeting (AGM), how special meetings are called, notice period, quorum and voting.
**Management committee and officers:** positions, how they are elected, term length, maximum number of terms, and how to remove them.
**Money:** share capital, bank account and signatories, spending limits, records, audit, and how surplus is allocated.
**Disputes and discipline:** the steps for complaints, fines and expulsion, and the right to be heard.
**Amendment and dissolution:** how bylaws are changed, and what happens to assets if the cooperative closes.

blocks.text: Authority flows upward from members

In a cooperative the highest authority is the general meeting of all members. The general meeting elects a management committee. The committee appoints or supervises officers and any staff who run daily work. Many cooperatives also elect a small supervisory or audit committee that checks the books on members' behalf. Write this chain into the bylaws so that nobody, not even the founder, sits above the general meeting.

blocks.title: Who answers to whom
items: General meeting of all members
Elected management committee
Supervisory or audit committee
Officers and staff
blocks.caption: The members at the top hold final power; every level below reports back to them.

blocks.text: Quorum and voting

A **quorum** is the minimum number of members who must be present for a meeting's decisions to count. Without one, three members could meet on a quiet afternoon and decide to sell the group's machine. An **ordinary resolution** passes by a simple majority of members present and voting. A **special resolution**, needed for serious matters, requires a larger majority, often two-thirds. Your bylaws should list which decisions are special. Common ones are changing the bylaws, borrowing above a set amount, selling major equipment, expelling a member, and dissolving the cooperative.

blocks.title: Worked example: setting quorum and a two-thirds rule
blocks.context: For example, a 24-member palm oil processing cooperative near Owerri is drafting its bylaws. The secretary, Ngozi, proposes a quorum of half the members plus one, and a two-thirds majority of members present for special resolutions.
steps: Quorum: half of 24 is 12, plus one is 13. At least 13 members must be present.
At the meeting, 18 members are present, so quorum is met.
The committee proposes buying a second press on credit, which the bylaws list as a special resolution.
Two-thirds of 18 present is 18 x 2 / 3 = 12. The motion needs at least 12 yes votes.
The vote is 13 yes, 4 no and 1 abstention. 13 is at least 12, so the motion passes.
Ngozi records in the minutes: members present, quorum met, motion text, and the vote count.
blocks.result: The decision is valid and recorded. If only 12 members had come, the meeting would have had no quorum and the press purchase would have had to wait for a properly called meeting.

blocks.text: Money rules that prevent most quarrels

items: All money goes into the cooperative's bank account. No officer keeps group money in a personal account.
Every payment needs two signatories or two approvals on the banking app, and the two must not be related or from the same household.
Spending limits: officers may spend up to a fixed amount per month for routine costs; above it, the committee decides; above a higher amount, the general meeting decides.
Every naira in or out is written in the cashbook with a receipt or bank reference, and any member may inspect the books on request.
Surplus is allocated each year by the general meeting according to the bylaw rule, for example a fixed percentage to reserves first.

blocks.title: Protect members' money from fraud
blocks.text: Never share the group account's banking app PIN or one-time passwords in the WhatsApp group, even with officers. Each signatory keeps her own login. Scammers often pose as bank staff or as a member who has "changed her number". Confirm any unusual payment request by a voice call to a number already saved, and report suspected fraud to your bank at once.

blocks.title: Limit terms of office
blocks.text: A rule such as "officers serve two years and may be re-elected once" gives new members a path into leadership and stops one person becoming the cooperative. Write it in before anyone has been in office long enough to resist it.

takeaways: Bylaws cover membership, meetings, officers, money, disputes, amendment and dissolution
The general meeting of all members is the highest authority
Set a quorum and list which decisions need a special resolution
All money goes through a group bank account with two signatories
Write term limits and spending limits in before anyone needs them

activity.title: Draft four key clauses
steps: Write your membership clause: who may join, entry share amount, and how a member leaves.
Calculate the quorum for your group size using half plus one, and write it down.
List four decisions that will need a two-thirds special resolution.
Write a spending limits table with three levels: officers, committee and general meeting.
Read the four clauses to two members and note their questions.
activity.evidence: A one-page draft with the four clauses, the quorum calculation and members' questions

quiz.q: Which phrase is part of the ICA definition of a cooperative?
options: A profit-making company owned by its largest investors
An autonomous association of persons united voluntarily
A government programme that supports small traders
A savings scheme run by a bank for its customers
quiz.explain: The ICA defines a cooperative as an autonomous association of persons united voluntarily to meet common needs through a jointly-owned and democratically-controlled enterprise.

quiz.q: Ada holds 10 shares in her primary cooperative and Tope holds 2. How many votes does each have at the general meeting?
options: Ada 10, Tope 2
Ada 5, Tope 1
One vote each
Only officers vote
quiz.explain: Principle 2, democratic member control: in primary cooperatives members have equal voting rights, one member, one vote.

quiz.q: A donor offers a grant on condition that it appoints the cooperative's treasurer. Which principle is most at risk?
options: Concern for community
Cooperation among cooperatives
Education, training and information
Autonomy and independence
quiz.explain: Principle 4 says agreements with outside bodies must ensure democratic control by members and keep the cooperative's autonomy.

quiz.q: A 30-member group wants a quorum of half plus one. What is the quorum?
quiz.explain: Half of 30 is 15, plus one is 16.

quiz.q: A women's sewing group wants a legal form that builds in one member, one vote and surplus shared by use of the business. Where should it register?
options: As a business name at the CAC
As a cooperative society with the state cooperative office
As incorporated trustees at the CAC
It does not need any written rules
quiz.explain: A cooperative society is registered with the state cooperative office and is designed around cooperative principles. A business name is not a separate legal person, and incorporated trustees are for non-profit purposes.

modules.title: Roles, Controls, Quality and the Group's Numbers
modules.overview: Turn the bylaws into daily practice. You will assign roles with clear separation of duties, write a standard operating procedure for an order, set a shared quality standard with internal checks, reconcile the bank account, and cost a bulk order and allocate its surplus fairly.

lessons.title: Roles, separation of duties and an order-to-cash procedure
objectives: Assign the core roles in a group enterprise with one named owner for each task
Apply separation of duties so no single person controls a whole money process
Write a step-by-step standard operating procedure (SOP) for taking and delivering an order
Rotate roles without losing accountability

blocks.text: In many groups, important tasks belong to "everybody", which in practice means nobody. The fabric is not ordered because each member thought another would do it. Or the opposite happens: one energetic member takes the order, collects the deposit, buys the materials and keeps the records alone. Even if she is completely honest, the group cannot see what happened, and suspicion grows. This lesson fixes both problems with named roles, separation of duties and a written procedure.

blocks.name: team-assignment
blocks.alt: A team leader assigning tasks on a board
blocks.caption: Every task has one named owner, even when many members help.

blocks.text: Core roles in a group enterprise

head: Role
Main duties
Must not also
rows: Leads meetings, represents the group, follows up decisions
Hold the cash or keep the cashbook
Notices of meetings, minutes, membership register, correspondence
Receives money into the bank account, pays approved bills, keeps receipts
Keep the cashbook she is checked against, or sign payments alone
Keeps the cashbook and members' accounts, prepares monthly statements
Plans work, assigns jobs to members, checks quality before delivery
Approve payment for work she inspected for her own household
Takes orders, confirms prices and dates in writing, handles complaints
Change agreed prices without committee approval

blocks.text: Separation of duties

**Separation of duties** means that the steps of any money process are split between at least two people, so that an error or a theft by one person is likely to be noticed by another. The classic split is: one person approves a payment, another makes it, and a third records it or checks the records. In a small group of 8 to 15 women you cannot always have three people, but you can always have two. The treasurer pays; the financial secretary records; the supervisory committee checks monthly that the two agree.

blocks.title: Controls protect the honest
blocks.text: Separation of duties is not an accusation. It protects an honest treasurer from being suspected, because the records show what happened. Explain it to members this way and it is accepted much more easily.
A standard operating procedure for an order

A **standard operating procedure (SOP)** is a short written list of the steps for a task that happens again and again, with who does each step. Write one for your most common money flow: from the moment a customer asks for a price to the moment the group is paid in full. Keep it to one page so it can be pinned up or shared as a picture on the group's WhatsApp.

blocks.title: Worked example: an order SOP for a catering group
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa's 9-member catering cooperative in Kaduna receives a request to supply 200 plates of jollof rice with chicken for a wedding, at 3,500 naira per plate (an illustrative price; check current local prices).
steps: Sales lead (Aisha) confirms the menu, quantity, date and price on WhatsApp and sends a written quote: 200 x 3,500 = 700,000 naira, 60 percent deposit to confirm.
Customer pays the deposit of 700,000 x 0.60 = 420,000 naira by transfer into the cooperative's bank account only. Aisha never accepts it into her own account.
Treasurer (Rakiya) confirms the credit on the bank app and tells the group the order is confirmed.
Financial secretary (Zainab) records the deposit in the cashbook and the order register, with the bank reference.
Production lead (Hauwa) writes the ingredient list and work rota. Purchases above the officers' limit are approved by a second committee member before Rakiya pays.
Production lead checks food safety on the day: clean hands, covered hair, food held hot, no member cooking while sick.
Balance of 280,000 naira is collected by transfer before the food is served, recorded by Zainab, and the customer gets a receipt.
blocks.result: Five different members touched the order, each with a clear duty. The money never passed through a personal account, every naira has a bank reference, and any member can trace the order from quote to full payment.

blocks.title: Order to cash, with owners
items: Quote in writing (sales)
Deposit into group account
Treasurer confirms payment
Bookkeeper records it
Production delivers to standard
Balance paid, receipt issued
blocks.caption: Each step has a different owner, so no one person controls the whole flow of money.

blocks.title: Food orders
blocks.text: For any group that cooks or processes food, add hygiene steps to the SOP: hand washing with soap, clean water, separating raw and cooked foods, cooking thoroughly and keeping food at safe temperatures. These follow the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food. A member with diarrhoea or vomiting should not handle food that day.
Rotating roles without losing accountability

Some groups rotate roles to share skills and avoid power building up in one person. That is healthy, provided each period has a named holder and a proper handover. When the treasurer changes, the outgoing and incoming treasurers, with one committee member, count any cash, print or screenshot the bank balance, agree the cashbook balance, and all three sign a short handover note. Without this, problems from the old term become arguments in the new one.

takeaways: Give every task one named owner, even when many members help
Split every money process between at least two people
Write a one-page SOP for your most common order, with an owner for each step
Customer money goes only into the group account, never a personal one
Hand over roles with a counted, signed balance

activity.title: Write your order SOP
steps: List your group's six core roles and write one member's name against each.
Check the table above: mark any member who currently holds two roles that should be separate.
Write a one-page SOP for your most common order, from quote to full payment, with an owner for each step.
Share it with members and ask each to confirm her own steps.
Pin it up or save it as the group's WhatsApp description or pinned message.
activity.evidence: A one-page SOP with named owners and a role list showing separated duties

lessons.title: A shared quality standard, internal checks and the monthly bank reconciliation
objectives: Write a product specification sheet that every member's work must meet
Run a simple inspection and a fair process when work falls short
Reconcile the group cashbook with the bank statement and explain any difference
Describe what a supervisory committee checks each month

blocks.text: A buyer who orders from a group expects the same quality whoever made the item. In a single-owner business, the standard lives in the owner's head. In a group it must be written down and checked, or one member's weak work damages everyone's name. The same is true of money: members trust the books only if someone other than the person keeping them checks them regularly. This lesson covers both kinds of check.

blocks.name: clipboard
blocks.caption: A written specification and a short inspection record make quality the same for every member's work.

blocks.text: The product specification sheet

A **specification sheet** describes exactly what a finished product must be. It should be specific enough that two members checking the same item would reach the same verdict. For a sewn school uniform, it might list: fabric type and colour code, measurements for each size with an allowed difference of about 1 cm, stitch type and stitches per inch, buttons sewn with a shank, no loose threads, pressed and folded, size label attached. For a food or cosmetic product, it includes the recipe, batch size, packing and labelling. Products sold packaged to the public in Nigeria may also need NAFDAC registration; check with NAFDAC before selling in shops.
Inspection and a fair process

items: The production lead, or a rotating inspector, checks a sample from each member's batch against the specification before delivery. For small orders, check every piece.
Record the result in an inspection log: date, member, number checked, number passed, fault found.
Return faulty pieces to the member privately with the specific fault named, for example "hem uneven by 2 cm", and a date to correct it.
If the same member fails twice in a row, the production lead pairs her with a stronger member for the next batch.
Repeated failure after support goes to the committee under the discipline clause in the bylaws, never to public criticism on WhatsApp.

blocks.title: The group quality cycle
items: Write the specification
Members produce
Inspect and record
Correct privately
Review at monthly meeting
blocks.caption: Each monthly review updates the specification, so quality improves batch by batch.

blocks.text: The monthly bank reconciliation

A **bank reconciliation** compares the group's own cashbook balance with the balance on the bank statement for the same date, and explains every difference. The two rarely match exactly, for honest reasons: bank charges and SMS alerts the bookkeeper has not yet recorded, a member's transfer that reached the bank but was not written in the cashbook, or a deposit made on the last day that the bank shows the next day. The job is to adjust both sides until they agree. If a difference remains that nobody can explain, it must be investigated before the meeting, not ignored.

blocks.title: Worked example: reconciling September
blocks.context: For example, Grace is on the supervisory committee of a 15-member uniform sewing cooperative in Jos. On 30 September the cashbook shows 412,500 naira, but the bank statement shows 389,000 naira.
steps: Bank charges and SMS fees on the statement, not in the cashbook: 1,500 naira. Cashbook adjusted: 412,500 - 1,500 = 411,000.
A member's share payment of 20,000 naira arrived in the bank but was not recorded. Cashbook adjusted: 411,000 + 20,000 = 431,000.
A deposit of 45,000 naira paid in on 30 September shows on the bank statement only on 1 October. Bank side adjusted: 389,000 + 45,000 = 434,000.
Difference remaining: 434,000 - 431,000 = 3,000 naira. Grace checks the cashbook line by line.
She finds a 3,000 naira payment for thread written twice. Removing the duplicate adds 3,000 back: 431,000 + 3,000 = 434,000.
Both sides now show 434,000 naira. Grace and the financial secretary both sign the reconciliation sheet.
blocks.result: The September books are reconciled at 434,000 naira, with every difference explained in writing. The bookkeeper corrects the duplicate entry and records the bank charges and the member's payment.

blocks.title: When a difference cannot be explained
blocks.text: If money is missing after checking every line, do not accuse anyone in the group chat. The supervisory committee writes down the facts, asks the officers concerned for an explanation in a private meeting, and reports to the next general meeting. If fraud is suspected, involve the bank and take advice from your state cooperative office.
What the supervisory committee checks each month

items: The bank reconciliation, signed by two people.
Every payment above the officers' limit has a recorded approval.
Receipts or bank references exist for a sample of payments.
Members' contribution and share records add up to the total in the cashbook.
The inspection log: number of pieces checked, passed and returned.
Any customer complaints and how they were resolved.

blocks.text: A registered cooperative will also have its accounts audited, and the cooperative authorities may inspect them. Groups that already reconcile every month find audit easy, because the evidence is already in order.

takeaways: Write a specification sheet clear enough that two inspectors reach the same verdict
Correct weak work privately, with the fault named and a date to fix it
Reconcile the cashbook with the bank statement every month and explain every difference
An unexplained difference is investigated in private and reported to the general meeting
Monthly checks make the annual audit straightforward

activity.title: Run one month's checks
steps: Write a specification sheet for your group's main product with at least six measurable points.
Inspect five finished pieces against it and record the results in an inspection log.
Take last month's cashbook balance and bank statement, and list every difference between them.
Adjust both sides and show whether they agree. If not, write what still needs to be checked.
Have a second member sign the reconciliation.
activity.evidence: A specification sheet, a five-line inspection log and a signed one-month bank reconciliation

lessons.title: Costing a bulk order, checking capacity and allocating the surplus
objectives: Cost a bulk group order line by line, including members' labour
Check whether the group's real capacity can meet the delivery date
Allocate a surplus to reserves, education and patronage according to the bylaws
Calculate each member's patronage refund in proportion to her transactions

blocks.text: Group money needs extra clarity because several households depend on it. The most common money quarrels in group enterprises are not about theft. They are about a price that did not cover costs, an order the group could not finish on time, or a surplus shared in a way some members felt was unfair. This lesson works through all three with one realistic order, using the cooperative rule for sharing surplus from Principle 3.

blocks.name: abacus
blocks.caption: Cost first, check capacity second, share surplus last, and write every figure down.

blocks.text: Step 1: Cost the whole order

List every cost the group will pay to deliver the order: materials, members' labour paid per piece or per day, transport, electricity or fuel for machines, packaging, and bank or payment fees. Members' labour is a real cost. If the price only covers materials, members are working for nothing and the surplus is an illusion. The difference between the order value and the total cost is the **surplus**.
Step 2: Check capacity honestly

Group capacity is not simply the sum of what each member can do alone. Coordination, waiting for shared machines, inspection and corrections all take time. Add a buffer of about 20 percent to the pure production time, and compare the result with the delivery date before saying yes.
Step 3: Allocate the surplus by the bylaws

The ICA's third principle says members allocate surpluses to developing the cooperative (possibly through reserves, at least part of which is indivisible), to benefiting members in proportion to their transactions with the cooperative, and to other activities the members approve. The payment to members in proportion to their transactions is often called a **patronage refund**. In a producers' group, a member's transactions can be the number of pieces she produced or the produce she supplied. Your bylaws fix the percentages. The ones below are illustrative choices for this example, not legal requirements; check whether your state's cooperative rules set a minimum reserve.

blocks.title: Worked example: 300 school uniform sets
blocks.context: For example, the 6 sewing members of Bisola's cooperative in Ibadan are offered an order of 300 uniform sets at 6,500 naira per set, delivery in 15 working days. All prices are illustrative; use your own current local prices.
steps: Order value: 300 x 6,500 = 1,950,000 naira.
Materials per set: fabric 2,400 + thread, buttons and zip 350 + packaging 100 = 2,850 naira. For 300 sets: 855,000 naira.
Sewing labour paid to members: 1,500 per set x 300 = 450,000 naira. Cutting: 200 per set x 300 = 60,000 naira.
Transport and delivery 40,000, fuel and machine maintenance 60,000, bank and transfer fees 5,000 naira.
Capacity: 6 members x 5 sets a day = 30 sets a day. 300 / 30 = 10 days, plus a 20 percent buffer = 12 days. That fits within 15 days, so the group accepts.
Allocation by the bylaws: reserve 25 percent = 120,000; education and training fund 5 percent = 24,000; patronage refund 70 percent = 336,000 naira. Check: 120,000 + 24,000 + 336,000 = 480,000.
Patronage per set: 336,000 / 300 = 1,120 naira for each set a member sewed.
blocks.result: The order makes a surplus of 480,000 naira. 120,000 builds the reserve, 24,000 pays for training, and 336,000 is returned to the six sewing members at 1,120 naira per set they produced, on top of the labour pay they already received.

blocks.text: Compare the two right-hand columns. An equal split gives each member 336,000 / 6 = 56,000 naira, so Shade, who sewed 30 sets, gets the same as Bisola, who sewed 70. The patronage method follows the cooperative principle of equity: members benefit in proportion to their transactions. Whichever method your group chooses, write it in the bylaws and apply it every time. Changing the rule after the money is known is one of the fastest ways to break a group.

blocks.title: Where the order money goes
items: Order value received
Pay all costs and labour
Surplus calculated
Reserve and education fund
Patronage refund to members
blocks.caption: Costs, including members' labour, are paid first; the surplus is shared only by the written rule.

blocks.title: Do not share money you have not received
blocks.text: Allocate the surplus only after the customer has paid in full and all bills are settled. Groups that share expected surplus early often find a late payment or a returned batch has left them short, with members already paid.

takeaways: Members' labour is a cost; include it before calculating surplus
Add about a 20 percent buffer to production time before accepting a delivery date
Under Principle 3, surplus goes to reserves, to members by their transactions, or to approved activities
A patronage refund rewards members in proportion to their use of or work for the cooperative
Write the allocation rule in the bylaws and never change it after the figures are known

activity.title: Cost and allocate a real order
steps: Choose a real or likely order for your group and write its quantity, price and delivery date.
List every cost line, including members' labour, and total it.
Calculate the surplus and check capacity with a 20 percent buffer.
Allocate the surplus using your bylaw percentages, or propose percentages for members to vote on.
Calculate each member's patronage refund and check that the column adds up to the patronage total.
activity.evidence: A costing sheet, a capacity check and a member-by-member surplus allocation that adds up

quiz.q: Aisha takes customer orders and also wants to receive deposits into her own account to save time. What should the group do?
options: Allow it if she is trusted
Require all deposits into the group account, confirmed by the treasurer
Let her keep the money until the order is finished
Ask customers to pay in cash only
quiz.explain: Separation of duties: the person who takes orders should not also receive the money, and group money never passes through a personal account.

quiz.q: The cashbook shows 250,000 naira and the bank statement 247,800 naira. The only difference found is unrecorded bank charges. How much are the charges?
options: 2,800 naira
1,200 naira
2,200 naira
22,000 naira
quiz.explain: 250,000 - 247,800 = 2,200 naira. Recording the charges brings the cashbook down to 247,800, matching the bank.

quiz.q: A member's batch fails inspection because hems are uneven. What is the best first step?
options: Return the pieces privately, name the fault and set a date to correct it
Post photos of the faults in the group chat
Quietly accept the pieces to avoid conflict
Expel her at the next meeting
quiz.explain: Faults are corrected privately with the specific problem named; repeated failure goes to the committee under the bylaws.

quiz.q: A surplus of 600,000 naira is allocated 25 percent reserve, 5 percent education, 70 percent patronage. 400 pieces were produced. What is the patronage refund per piece?
options: 1,500 naira
1,125 naira
1,000 naira
1,050 naira
quiz.explain: 70 percent of 600,000 is 420,000. 420,000 / 400 = 1,050 naira per piece.

quiz.q: A group can produce 40 pieces a day. A customer wants 400 pieces in 10 working days. Using a 20 percent buffer, what should the group do?
options: Accept, because 400 / 40 = 10 days exactly
Accept and work longer hours without planning
Negotiate a later date or smaller quantity, because 10 days plus 20 percent is 12 days
Refuse all future orders from this customer
quiz.explain: Pure production time is 10 days; with a 20 percent buffer it is 12 days, which is more than 10. Negotiate before accepting.

modules.title: Growth, Members and Community: Contracts, Member Lifecycle and the AGM
modules.overview: Grow without losing control of your cooperative. You will test a big buyer's offer for cash flow and autonomy, manage the full member lifecycle from admission to exit, and run an annual general meeting that reports honestly and sets the group's 90-day governance plan.

lessons.title: Big buyers, partners and funders: growing without losing autonomy
objectives: Calculate the working capital a large order with delayed payment really needs
Spot contract terms that threaten the cooperative's autonomy or cash
Prepare a counter-offer that the group can safely deliver
Explain how working with other cooperatives (Principle 6) can add capacity

blocks.text: A well-run group is attractive to bigger buyers, distributors and programmes, because it offers more capacity than a single producer. That attention is good news, but large offers often come with terms that can sink a small cooperative: long payment delays, exclusivity, penalties, or a partner who wants a say in how the group is run. Principle 4 says any agreement with an outside organisation must keep democratic control by the members and the cooperative's autonomy. This lesson shows how to test an offer before members vote on it.

blocks.name: handshake-deal
blocks.alt: Two people shaking hands on a deal
blocks.caption: A good deal is one the group can deliver, afford to wait for, and still control.

blocks.text: Four questions for every big offer

items: **Cash:** How much must the group spend before the first payment arrives? Do we have it, without borrowing at high cost?
**Capacity:** Can we produce this quantity, to the standard, with a 20 percent time buffer?
**Control:** Does any clause give the partner power over our members, officers, prices to others, or bylaws?
**Exit:** Can either side end the agreement with reasonable notice, and what happens to goods already made?

blocks.text: Working capital: the hidden cost of delayed payment

**Working capital** is the money the group needs to keep producing while it waits to be paid. When a buyer pays 60 days after delivery, the group may have to fund two or three months of production from its own pocket. Many groups look only at the margin per piece and forget to ask whether they can survive the wait.

blocks.title: Worked example: testing a fashion retailer's offer
blocks.context: For example, Kemi's adire cooperative in Abeokuta, now registered, is offered a contract by a retailer: 300 pieces a month at 9,000 naira each, payment 60 days after each delivery, and the group may not sell to any other shop. The group's cost is 6,500 naira per piece and its working capital is 1,500,000 naira. Prices are illustrative.
steps: Monthly production cost: 300 x 6,500 = 1,950,000 naira, which is already more than the group's 1,500,000.
Month 1's delivery is paid at the end of month 3. By then the group has funded 3 months: 3 x 1,950,000 = 5,850,000 naira.
The exclusivity clause would also stop sales to the group's existing customers, which threatens its independence.
Counter-offer drafted by the committee: 150 pieces a month, 30 percent deposit with each order, balance 30 days after delivery, no exclusivity, either side may end with 30 days' notice.
New order value: 150 x 9,000 = 1,350,000 naira. Deposit: 30 percent = 405,000. Cost: 150 x 6,500 = 975,000.
Net cash out per month: 975,000 - 405,000 = 570,000. Two months before the first balance arrives: 2 x 570,000 = 1,140,000 naira, within the 1,500,000 available.
Margin: 150 x (9,000 - 6,500) = 375,000 naira a month.
blocks.result: The original offer needed 5,850,000 naira of funding and took away the group's freedom to sell elsewhere. The counter-offer needs at most 1,140,000, keeps existing customers and still earns 375,000 naira a month. The committee takes both versions to a general meeting for a vote.

blocks.title: Sorting offers by value and control
items: High value, members keep control: pursue
High value, partner takes control: renegotiate
Low value, members keep control: only if easy
Low value, partner takes control: decline
blocks.caption: An attractive offer that takes control away from members should be renegotiated, not signed as it stands.

blocks.text: Terms to read twice

items: **Exclusivity:** stops you selling to others. Accept only with higher volumes, guaranteed for a fixed period.
**Penalties for late delivery:** check the amount and that it also applies to the buyer's late payment.
**Rejection of goods:** the buyer's quality standard should be written and match your specification sheet.
**Governance conditions from funders:** a funder may ask for reports and audits, which is reasonable, but should not appoint your officers or change your bylaws.
**Who signs:** only officers authorised by a committee or general meeting resolution, as your bylaws require.

blocks.text: Growing through cooperation among cooperatives

If an order is too big, Principle 6 offers another route: partner with another cooperative instead of overstretching your own. Two groups can split an order under a written agreement covering quality standard, share of the quantity, how payment flows, and who answers to the buyer. Cooperatives can also join together in a secondary body, often called a union, to buy inputs in bulk or market together. Ask your state cooperative office which unions operate in your sector.

blocks.title: Offers that are too good
blocks.text: Be cautious of "buyers" or "grant agents" who ask the group to pay a registration, processing or approval fee before an order or grant is released. Verify the organisation independently, never pay fees to a personal account, and take any such request to the committee before acting.

takeaways: Test every big offer on cash, capacity, control and exit
Delayed payment means the group funds production in advance; calculate it
Counter-offer with deposits, shorter payment terms and no exclusivity when needed
Agreements must keep democratic member control (Principle 4)
Partnering with another cooperative can add capacity without overstretching (Principle 6)

activity.title: Test an offer
steps: Write down a real or likely offer: quantity, price, payment terms and any special clauses.
Calculate the monthly cost and the total the group must fund before the first payment.
Compare that figure with the group's available working capital.
Mark each clause as acceptable, needs change, or reject, using the four questions.
Draft a counter-offer and recalculate the cash needed.
activity.evidence: A one-page offer test with the working capital calculation and a drafted counter-offer

lessons.title: The member lifecycle: admission, education, discipline and exit
objectives: Run a fair admission and induction process for new members
Plan member education as Principle 5 requires
Use a step-by-step ladder for disputes and discipline
Calculate what a leaving member is owed and why reserves stay with the cooperative

blocks.text: A cooperative is a group of peers, not a boss and workers. Leadership here rests on fair process and earned respect. Most serious crises in group enterprises can be traced to a weak point in the member lifecycle: a new member who never understood the rules, a quarrel left to grow for months, or a member who leaves and feels cheated. This lesson walks through each stage and gives you a calculation for a fair exit.

blocks.name: welcome-aboard
blocks.alt: A person welcoming a new team member
blocks.caption: A clear welcome and induction prevent many later disputes.

blocks.text: Admission and induction

items: The applicant reads the bylaws and the current group agreement, or has them read to her in her preferred language.
She completes an application form, which the secretary records in the membership register.
The committee or general meeting decides by the rule in the bylaws, applying the same criteria to every applicant, as Principle 1 requires.
She pays the entry fee and share capital into the group account and receives a receipt.
An experienced member takes her through the SOP, the specification sheet and the money rules in her first month.
At the end of the first month the production lead and the new member review her work together.

blocks.text: Education as a duty, not a favour

Principle 5 says cooperatives provide education and training for members, elected representatives, managers and employees, so they can contribute effectively to the cooperative's development. In practice, budget for it from the education fund set aside from surplus. Typical needs are bookkeeping for the treasurer and financial secretary, quality training for new producers, and short sessions for all members on reading the monthly statement. A member who can read the accounts is far less likely to suspect the officers without reason. Principle 5 also asks cooperatives to inform the public, particularly young people and opinion leaders, about the nature and benefits of cooperation. A short talk at a church, mosque or community meeting, explaining how your group works, is one practical way to do this, and it often brings in good new members.
The dispute and discipline ladder

Write a ladder into the bylaws and climb it one step at a time. Most issues end on the first or second step. Skipping straight to expulsion, or to a public argument in the WhatsApp group, usually makes things worse and can be challenged as unfair.

blocks.title: The dispute ladder
items: Private conversation
Mediation by a neutral member
Committee hearing, both sides heard
Written warning or sanction
General meeting decides expulsion
blocks.caption: Each step is recorded; the member always has the right to be heard before a sanction.

blocks.title: The right to be heard
blocks.text: Before any sanction, tell the member in writing what she is accused of, give her a reasonable time to respond, and let her speak at the hearing. Record the decision and the reasons in the minutes. A process that skips this can split the group even when the accusation is true.
Exit: what a leaving member is owed

Members leave for many reasons: moving to another city, family needs, or disagreement. The bylaws should say what she receives and when. Usually she gets back her paid-up share capital, plus any patronage refund already declared but not yet paid, minus any money she owes the cooperative. Principle 3 notes that reserves are developed by the cooperative and that at least part of them should be indivisible. That means a leaving member does not take a share of the reserve fund. It stays to protect the members who remain.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ronke leaves the sewing cooperative
blocks.context: For example, Ronke is moving from Ibadan to Abuja and resigns from Bisola's cooperative. The bylaws say a leaving member is paid within 90 days of the committee accepting her resignation.
steps: Paid-up share capital, confirmed in the members' ledger: 25,000 naira.
Patronage refund declared at the last general meeting and not yet paid: 18,400 naira.
Money she owes: the balance of an advance for a machine part, 12,000 naira.
Reserve fund: no share, because the bylaws make the reserve indivisible.
The financial secretary prepares a statement; Ronke and two officers sign it; the treasurer pays 31,400 naira by transfer to Ronke's own account and records the reference.
blocks.result: Ronke receives 31,400 naira with a signed statement showing exactly how it was calculated. Her name is removed from the membership register and the group's bank mandate if she was a signatory, and she leaves on good terms.

blocks.title: Plan exits so the group survives them
blocks.text: If several members could leave at once, paying out all their share capital might empty the account. Some bylaws allow payment in instalments or within a set period. Decide this calmly in the bylaws, not in the middle of a crisis.

Finally, mark successes together. When a big order is delivered or the audit comes back clean, say so at the meeting and record it in the minutes. Members who see shared success stay committed through the hard months.

takeaways: Apply the same written admission criteria to every applicant
Fund member education from the education fund, as Principle 5 expects
Climb the dispute ladder one step at a time and always let the member be heard
A leaving member gets her share capital and declared refunds, minus what she owes
The indivisible reserve stays with the cooperative

activity.title: Map your member lifecycle
steps: Write your admission steps and the criteria the committee will use.
List three training needs for the next year and who will deliver each.
Write your group's dispute ladder with the person responsible at each step.
Calculate an exit amount for a sample member using real figures from your ledger.
Check that your bylaws say what happens to the reserve when a member leaves.
activity.evidence: A one-page member lifecycle plan with an admission checklist, dispute ladder and a sample exit calculation

lessons.title: The AGM, the annual report to members and your 90-day governance plan
objectives: Prepare a clear agenda and notice for an annual general meeting
Present the year's results and the surplus allocation in a form members understand
Show concern for community through a member-approved policy
Write a 90-day plan that closes the group's biggest governance gap

blocks.text: The annual general meeting (AGM) is where the members, the highest authority in the cooperative, receive the accounts, approve the surplus allocation, elect officers and set direction. A well-run AGM is the clearest evidence that a group is a real cooperative and not a private business with members as helpers. This final lesson brings the course together: the report, the decisions and the plan that comes out of the meeting.

blocks.name: meeting
blocks.alt: People seated around a table in a meeting
blocks.caption: At the AGM, the members review the year and decide together.

blocks.text: Notice and agenda

Send written notice to every member within the period your bylaws require, with the agenda and a short summary of the accounts, so members can read before the meeting. Share it on WhatsApp and also on paper for members who rely on it. Check quorum at the start and record it.

items: Opening, confirmation of quorum and adoption of the agenda.
Approval of the minutes of the last general meeting.
Chairperson's report on the year's activities.
Presentation of the accounts and the supervisory or audit committee's report.
Approval of the surplus allocation as the bylaws provide.
Election of officers whose terms have ended.
Plan and budget for the coming year, including the 90-day governance plan.
Any other business notified in advance, then close.

blocks.text: The annual report in plain numbers

blocks.title: Worked example: the adire cooperative's year
blocks.context: For example, Kemi's 15-member adire cooperative in Abeokuta prepares its report for the AGM. The bylaws allocate surplus as: reserve 25 percent, education 5 percent, community 5 percent, patronage refund 65 percent. Figures are illustrative.
steps: Total sales for the year: 14,600,000 naira. Total costs, including members' labour: 12,350,000 naira.
Reserve 25 percent: 562,500 naira. Education 5 percent: 112,500 naira. Community 5 percent: 112,500 naira.
Members produced 1,950 pieces in the year, so the refund is 1,462,500 / 1,950 = 750 naira per piece produced.
The supervisory committee confirms that all 12 monthly bank reconciliations were signed.
blocks.result: Members see one page: sales, costs, surplus, the four-way allocation that adds back to 2,250,000 naira, and the refund rate of 750 naira per piece, which each member can multiply by her own production to check her refund.

blocks.name: ballot-box-with-ballot
blocks.caption: Officers are elected by members, one member, one vote.

blocks.text: Running a fair election

Elections are where Principle 2 becomes visible. Announce which offices are vacant in the notice, so members can prepare. At the meeting, invite nominations, and let each candidate speak briefly. Choose two members who are not candidates to count the votes. Use a secret ballot on slips of paper when the post is contested, so nobody feels pressure to vote with a powerful relative or neighbour. Each member present has one vote, whatever her shares or how long she has been a member. The secretary records the names of candidates, votes for each and the winner in the minutes. Outgoing officers then hand over records, cash and bank access with a counted, signed handover note within an agreed period, for example two weeks, and the bank mandate is updated at once.
Concern for community

Principle 7 asks cooperatives to work for the sustainable development of their communities through policies approved by their members. The key words are "approved by their members". In the example, the 112,500 naira community fund is not spent by the chairperson's choice; the AGM votes on a proposal, such as paying the training costs of two young women from the community as apprentices with the group. Record the decision and report next year on what it achieved.
Your 90-day governance plan

End the AGM by agreeing the group's single biggest governance gap and a 90-day plan to close it. Use the principles score from Lesson 1.1 and the readiness score from Lesson 1.2 to choose. Typical gaps are: no group bank account with two signatories, officers never elected, no written surplus rule, or no monthly reconciliation. Each action needs an owner, a date and a piece of evidence that proves it is done.

blocks.title: A 90-day governance plan
items: Days 1 to 15: agree the gap
Days 16 to 45: draft and consult
Days 46 to 60: vote at meeting
Days 61 to 90: apply and check
Day 90: report to members
blocks.caption: Every stage ends with something members can see: a draft, a vote, a record or a report.

head: Action
Owner
By day
Evidence
rows: Draft clause shared with all members
Special general meeting to vote on the rule
Minutes with quorum and vote count
Open group account with two signatories
First monthly reconciliation in new format
One-page update on WhatsApp and paper

blocks.title: Keep one governance file
blocks.text: Keep the bylaws, membership register, minutes, reconciliations, AGM reports and contracts in one file, on paper and as photos or scans in a shared folder that at least two officers can open. A funder, auditor or new officer can then understand the group in an hour.

takeaways: The AGM is where members receive accounts, approve the surplus allocation and elect officers
Present a one-page report whose allocation adds back exactly to the surplus
Community spending follows a policy approved by members (Principle 7)
Close one governance gap at a time with a 90-day plan of owners, dates and evidence
Keep all governance documents in one file that two officers can access

activity.title: Prepare your AGM pack
steps: Write an AGM notice and agenda for your group using the eight items above.
Prepare a one-page report: sales, costs, surplus and the allocation by your bylaw percentages.
Check with a calculator that the allocation adds back exactly to the surplus.
Write one community proposal for members to vote on.
Choose your biggest governance gap and write a five-line 90-day plan with owners, dates and evidence.
activity.evidence: An AGM notice, a one-page annual report with a checked allocation, and a 90-day governance plan

quiz.q: A buyer offers 200 pieces a month at a cost to the group of 5,000 naira each, paying 60 days after each delivery. Roughly how much must the group fund before month 1's payment arrives at the end of month 3?
options: 500,000 naira
quiz.explain: Monthly cost is 200 x 5,000 = 1,000,000 naira. Three months of production are funded before the first payment: 3,000,000 naira.

quiz.q: A funder offers a grant if it can approve every change to the cooperative's bylaws. What is the best response?
options: Accept, because grants are free money
Let the chairperson decide privately
Accept but hide the condition from members
Negotiate to remove the condition, since agreements must keep democratic member control
quiz.explain: Principle 4 requires that agreements with outside organisations keep democratic control by members and the cooperative's autonomy.

quiz.q: Uche leaves the cooperative. Share capital 30,000, declared unpaid refund 9,000, she owes 5,000. The reserve fund is 400,000. What is she owed?
options: 34,000 naira
44,000 naira
39,000 naira
34,000 naira plus a share of the reserve
quiz.explain: 30,000 + 9,000 - 5,000 = 34,000 naira. The reserve is indivisible and stays with the cooperative.

quiz.q: Two members quarrel over who caused a late delivery. What should happen first under the dispute ladder?
options: Expulsion vote at the next general meeting
A private conversation to resolve it
A public discussion in the WhatsApp group
A written warning to both
quiz.explain: The ladder starts with a private conversation, then mediation, then a committee hearing; most disputes end at the first steps.

quiz.q: At the AGM, who decides how the community fund is spent?
options: The chairperson alone
The largest customer
The members, by approving a policy or proposal
The bank
quiz.explain: Principle 7: cooperatives work for the sustainable development of their communities through policies approved by their members.

finalQuiz.q: Which of these is one of the six cooperative values in the ICA statement?
options: Competition
Solidarity
Seniority
Secrecy
finalQuiz.explain: The six values are self-help, self-responsibility, democracy, equality, equity and solidarity.

finalQuiz.q: Principle 1, voluntary and open membership, means a cooperative should:
options: Admit only relatives of founders
Admit anyone, even those who refuse member responsibilities
Be open to all who can use its services and accept membership responsibilities, without discrimination
Charge higher fees to members of other religions
finalQuiz.explain: The ICA wording: open to all persons able to use the services and willing to accept the responsibilities of membership, without gender, social, racial, political or religious discrimination.

finalQuiz.q: Where is a cooperative society registered in Nigeria?
options: The Corporate Affairs Commission as a business name
The state government's cooperative office
NAFDAC
The local market association
finalQuiz.explain: Cooperative societies are registered with the state cooperative office. The CAC registers business names, companies and incorporated trustees.

finalQuiz.q: A group scores 9 out of 16 on the readiness scorecard. Using the course's rule of thumb, what should it do?
options: Register immediately
Fix its gaps for about 90 days before registering or taking a big order
Disband the group
Ignore the score
finalQuiz.explain: 8 to 11 means spend about 90 days fixing gaps first; 12 or more means ready to move forward.

finalQuiz.q: A 20-member cooperative has 15 members present. A special resolution needs two-thirds of those present. How many yes votes are needed?
finalQuiz.explain: Two-thirds of 15 is 15 x 2 / 3 = 10 yes votes.

finalQuiz.q: Which pair of duties should NOT be held by the same person?
options: Taking minutes and keeping the membership register
Leading meetings and representing the group
Receiving customer money and keeping the cashbook it is checked against
Planning production and checking quality before delivery
finalQuiz.explain: Separation of duties: the person who handles money should not also keep the records that check her.

finalQuiz.q: The cashbook shows 300,000 naira. The bank shows 280,000. A 20,000 naira deposit made on the last day shows only next month. What is the reconciled position?
options: Both sides agree at 300,000 naira
20,000 naira is missing
The bank owes the group 40,000 naira
The cashbook must be reduced to 280,000
finalQuiz.explain: Adding the 20,000 deposit in transit to the bank side gives 300,000, which matches the cashbook.

finalQuiz.q: An order brings 900,000 naira in sales. Materials cost 420,000, members' labour 250,000 and transport 30,000. What is the surplus?
options: 480,000 naira
200,000 naira
650,000 naira
170,000 naira

finalQuiz.q: Principle 3 says surplus can be returned to members:
options: Equally to every member regardless of use
Only to officers
Only to the member with the most share capital
In proportion to their transactions with the cooperative
finalQuiz.explain: One of the three purposes in Principle 3 is benefiting members in proportion to their transactions with the cooperative, often called a patronage refund.

finalQuiz.q: A buyer asks for exclusivity and 60-day payment for an order larger than the group's working capital. What is the best move?
options: Sign quickly before the buyer changes her mind
Borrow from a lender with unknown terms
Counter-offer a smaller quantity, a deposit, shorter payment terms and no exclusivity
Refuse to discuss terms
finalQuiz.explain: Calculate the cash needed, then counter-offer terms the group can fund while keeping its freedom to sell to others.

finalQuiz.q: When a member leaves, what happens to the indivisible reserve?
options: It is shared among leaving members
It stays with the cooperative
It goes to the chairperson
It is paid to the state
finalQuiz.explain: Principle 3 refers to reserves, at least part of which would be indivisible; a leaving member does not take a share of them.

finalQuiz.q: Which item belongs on an AGM agenda?
options: Approval of the surplus allocation and election of officers
A private meeting of the founder and her family
Changing prices for one customer without a vote
Spending the community fund before members discuss it
finalQuiz.explain: The AGM receives the accounts, approves the surplus allocation and elects officers whose terms have ended.

capstone.title: Group Enterprise Governance Plan
capstone.brief: Produce a governance pack for a real cooperative or group enterprise: a principles and readiness assessment, draft bylaws, a role and money control system, a costed order with a checked surplus allocation, and a 90-day plan to close the group's biggest governance gap.
steps: Score the group against the seven ICA principles (out of 14) and the readiness scorecard (out of 16).
Draft bylaws covering membership, meetings with quorum, officers and terms, money and spending limits, surplus allocation, disputes and exit.
Name the holder of each core role, mark separated duties, and write a one-page order SOP.
Write a specification sheet and complete one month's signed bank reconciliation.
Cost one real order, check capacity with a 20 percent buffer and allocate the surplus member by member.
Write a 90-day governance plan with owners, dates and evidence, and present it at a members' meeting.
evidence: Principles score sheet and readiness scorecard
Draft bylaws or written group agreement read by members
Role list, order SOP and specification sheet
Costing sheet and surplus allocation that adds up exactly
90-day governance plan and minutes of the meeting where it was presented
